Summary:
THE POINT
All four answers in one place. If the room only remembers one slide, it should be this one.

THE PROOF
- Q1: fee checks up 13%; 42% of money (£165.7M of £393.6M) goes to Wise directly; 35% (£138.6M) because of app limits.
- Q2: 0.3% fee, £1 minimum, £15 cap, tested against a control group.
- Q3: 4,220 of 25,240 PartnerBank customers on Wise (17%) already use a multi-currency account.
- Q4: base case adds £724k of new revenue but does not pay back in 3 years, so pilot first.

WHY IT MATTERS
The headline: PartnerBank is growing with us, and the biggest opportunity is the money its own customers already send through Wise. Most of it leaves for reasons we can fix together.
Momentum:
THE POINT
The integration is working: more customers use it every month, and most of them complete a transfer.

THE PROOF
- Total Integration Users: 11,260 a month in April 2025 to 12,680 in March 2026, +13%.
- Total Active Users: 76% of people who checked the fee went on to send. A high conversion rate means the price and speed are competitive.
- December peaks (holiday sending). February rises after the UK tax-return deadline on 31 January.

WHY IT MATTERS
Start with a win the bank can take to its own leadership. It builds trust before we talk about the gap.

A LIKELY QUESTION
Customers are counted once per month, so the yearly total is not the sum of the months.
Service quality:
THE POINT
Reliability is not the problem. That rules out the easy excuse and points the conversation at product limits.

THE PROOF
- 96.6% of transfers started in the app completed.
- 77% of completed transfers arrived in under 20 seconds. Wise reports about 77% instant arrivals across its business, so the bank gets the same speed.
- The fee quote appears in 179 ms (median), so it feels instant to customers.

WHY IT MATTERS
Customers aren't leaving because the service is slow or unreliable. So when we look at why money goes elsewhere, we can focus on what the app does not offer yet.
The opportunity:
THE POINT
The bank's own customers already send a lot of money through Wise directly. That is growth the bank can capture, without finding new customers.

THE PROOF
- Transaction Volume: £227.9M through the app vs £165.7M on Wise directly, paid from PartnerBank accounts. 42% goes around the app.
- Total Wise Users from the Partner grew 31%, 2.4x the 13% growth in the app.
- The doughnut shows the full year: every pound PartnerBank customers sent, split by where they sent it.

WHY IT MATTERS
You keep the customer but lose the transaction, and any fee on it. This is the cheapest growth available: your customers already want to send this money. The question is why they do it outside your app.

A LIKELY QUESTION
Is this bad news for Wise? No. Wise earns either way, but money through the integration deepens the partnership and the bank's commitment to the platform.
Why it leaves:
THE POINT
Most of the money leaves for a specific, fixable reason. This turns the gap into a to-do list.

THE PROOF
- Over £50,000: £58.7M from about 940 customers. Few people, very large transfers.
- Currency not offered: £37.8M from about 11,600 customers. The most people affected.
- Sent from euros or dollars: £22.1M. The app only sends from pounds.
- Business customers: £20.0M. The app is personal-only.
- Not limits (grey): £14.8M could have gone through the app (an awareness issue), and £12.3M is accounts and cards (Question 3).

WHY IT MATTERS
35% of everything your customers send leaves because of four limits. Each one has a clear fix, and the data tells us which to do first.

A LIKELY QUESTION
How is each transfer counted once? Each gets one reason, checked in a fixed order: business, other source currency, same currency, missing currency, over £50,000, other product. Same-currency transfers did not appear in this data.
Currency coverage:
THE POINT
We don't need to add all 18 missing currencies at once. Three of them carry most of the money.

THE PROOF
- £37.8M a year went to the 18 currencies the integration does not support.
- Pakistani rupee £14.7M (39%), Bangladeshi taka £6.4M (17%), Japanese yen £6.2M (16%). Together 72%.
- They are also the most populous countries on the brief's missing list: Pakistan about 240M people, Bangladesh 172M, Japan 125M.
- Pakistan and Bangladesh have large UK communities who send money home regularly, so the demand is steady, not one-off.

WHY IT MATTERS
Add three currencies and you capture almost three-quarters of this gap. It is a focused, low-risk first step.
Activation:
THE POINT
There is a second opportunity that needs no new features: customers who signed up but never sent.

THE PROOF
- New Users Created: 24,720 this year.
- Total New Active Users: 12,240 made a first transfer (50%).
- 12,480 people have already said yes to the product and stopped before sending.
- Each 10-point improvement in that rate adds about 2,472 new senders a year.

WHY IT MATTERS
These customers already chose the product. Getting them to a first transfer is cheaper than winning new ones. Show the fee and arrival time up front, let them save a recipient, and remind them a few days after sign-up.

A LIKELY QUESTION
The dataset flags new users by month, not by sign-up date, so this is not a full cohort analysis. With sign-up dates I would track time to first transfer.
What we recommend:
THE POINT
Four priorities, ranked by money and by how many customers they reach, each with one KPI we review at every QBR.

THE PROOF
- The £76.7M: half of the four limits plus the money that could already have gone through the app (£153.4M in total). Accounts and cards are left out.
- 1. Missing currencies: £37.8M and the most customers (about 11,600).
- 2. The £50,000 limit: the most money (£58.7M) but only about 940 customers, and it likely needs risk and compliance input.
- 3. Send from euros and dollars: £22.1M from balances customers already hold.
- 4. First-transfer journey: 12,480 sign-ups waiting.

WHY IT MATTERS
This is the ask: agree these four priorities, and we track one number together every quarter, the share of your customers' money that goes through your app. The fee PartnerBank earns on this money is set in Question 2.

A LIKELY QUESTION
Why currencies before the £50,000 limit, when the limit is bigger? It reaches 12 times as many customers and is a more predictable build. The final order also depends on effort and compliance, which I would confirm with both product teams.
Fee design:
THE POINT
The fee can be set so most customers still pay less than at the big UK banks.

THE PROOF
- Design: 0.3% of the transfer, never less than £1, never more than £15.
- A percentage is fair because it scales with the amount. The minimum covers the fixed cost of tiny transfers. The cap protects large transfers: £10,000 pays £15, not £30.
- HSBC charges £5 and Lloyds £9.50 on non-euro payments (UK websites, checked 2 Nov 2026). PartnerBank is cheaper than HSBC below £1,667 and cheaper than Lloyds below £3,167.
- The median app transfer is about £1,500, so the typical customer pays less than at HSBC.

WHY IT MATTERS
The bank earns on every transfer and stays cheaper than HSBC and Lloyds for most customers. And a £0 fee isn't free: banks also earn on the exchange rate, so the fair test is how much the recipient gets.
Effect on usage:
THE POINT
The fee will earn money, but we do not know how many customers it will push away. The honest answer is to test it, not guess.

THE PROOF
- Small transfers feel it most: £1 is 2% of a £50 transfer. But only 3% of app transfers are £250 or less.
- If nobody stopped sending, the fee earns about £562k a year (average £5.98 per transfer). If 10 in 100 transfers stop, about £506k.
- The biggest risk is customers moving to Wise directly or another provider, which grows the gap from Question 1.
- New customers are usually the most price-sensitive, so first transfers need the closest watch.

WHY IT MATTERS
I'd recommend a controlled test. Split customers at random, not transfers, so each person always sees the same price. Show the full cost before they confirm, run it for at least two months to see repeat sending, and agree stop rules in advance.

A LIKELY QUESTION
Why not just launch and watch? Seasonality (December, February) would hide the fee's effect. A no-fee control group is the only clean comparison.
KPIs:
THE POINT
Fee income alone would make any fee look good. The real test is extra revenue after the customers who stop, with guardrails on customer health.

THE PROOF
- Fee check to send rate: today 76%. The first place a fee shows up.
- First-transfer rate: today 50%. New customers are the most sensitive.
- Transfers and money per customer: do people send less often, or save up and batch payments?
- Customers moving to Wise directly: the leakage already sized in Question 1.
- Complaints and support contacts per 1,000 transfers: do customers understand the fee?
- Extra revenue per customer: the decision metric, including customers who stopped.

WHY IT MATTERS
Every KPI is compared fee group vs no-fee group. The decision rule is simple: keep the fee only if extra revenue is positive and the guardrails stay within agreed limits.
Evidence:
THE POINT
Demand is not hypothetical. A meaningful share of the bank's customers already hold foreign currency, just outside the bank.

THE PROOF
- Product used: 4,220 of the 25,240 PartnerBank customers on Wise directly (17%) already use a Wise multi-currency account.
- 7,640 use an account, a card or receive money on Wise.
- Surveys measure intent, which usually overstates real adoption. This is revealed behaviour, which is stronger evidence.
- Wise could also share, in aggregate: how often they use it, which currencies they hold, and typical balances, to size what the bank is missing.

WHY IT MATTERS
Your survey says customers are interested. Our data shows thousands of them already do it, outside your bank. That is a ready-made pilot group.

A LIKELY QUESTION
Isn't that group biased? Yes: they already chose Wise, so they are keener than the average customer. Use them to design and test the pilot, not to forecast adoption across the whole bank.
Wise internal:
THE POINT
Counting all account revenue would overstate the case. Some of these customers already earn Wise money, so only the difference counts.

THE PROOF
- Assumptions (editable in the app): 3 partners, 100,000 eligible customers each, 5% open an account over 6 months after a 6-month build.
- Revenue £2.50 per account per month, minus £0.50 Wise already earns from these customers.
- Costs: £300k build, £20k launch per partner, £0.75 a month per account to run, £5k a month shared, £3 to activate an account.
- Base: £724k new revenue in 3 years, ending £-102k after costs. No payback yet.
- Upside (50% more adoption, 25% more revenue): pays back in month 22. Downside (half the adoption, 25% less revenue, 3-month delay): ends £-415k.

WHY IT MATTERS
The case is not proven on today's assumptions, and it swings on two numbers: adoption and revenue per account. That is exactly what a pilot can measure cheaply.
Wise internal 2:
THE POINT
Don't say yes or no to the full build. Buy the evidence first with a small, time-boxed pilot.

THE PROOF
- Cost and payback: from the model on the previous slide.
- Delivery effort: engineering months, and what it delays.
- Regulatory and fraud risk: holding balances brings safeguarding and licensing work that sending money does not.
- Confidence: Question 3 gives real behaviour, but from a keen group.
- Opportunity cost: the Send Money limits from Question 1 are already sized at £138.6M of money leaving the app, so compare revenue per engineering month.

WHY IT MATTERS
Fund discovery and one partner pilot. Agree targets up front for adoption, new revenue per account, and reliability and fraud. Decide go or stop after six months. That limits the downside and gives us real numbers for the full case.
Appendix:
THE POINT
The numbers are illustrative, but the method is sound and ready for real data.

THE PROOF
- 10,000 records built to cover all 12 data points in the brief.
- Scaling: the brief shows about 33,000 customers checking the fee in a quarter; the sample had 1,608, so counts and money are x20. Percentages, averages and the £50,000 and fee rules use real transfer sizes.
- With real data I would ask first for: a link between each fee check and its transfer, sign-up dates, the partner contract (fee share and costs), and the reasons customers give for leaving.

WHY IT MATTERS
Only use this slide if asked how the numbers were made.
